blocks.cap: The kitchen of the Uedera flat before four in the morning

blocks.p: The plate was still upside down on the counter.

Rei stood in the dark kitchen and looked at it. A white plate turned over a second plate, the way he had left it at nine o'clock. Under it was rice and the ginger pork Gin liked, gone cold and grey. Nobody had lifted it. Nobody had eaten.
He was holding the kettle. He did not remember picking it up. The clock on the stove said 3:47.

The flat was very quiet. It was two small rooms and a kitchen, built for two people, and tonight it held only one. Outside, Tokyo had reached the hour when even the trucks go quiet. Somewhere below, a vending machine hummed on the corner of the street. There was one on almost every corner in the city, lit up all night, selling cold tea and canned coffee to nobody.

It was August 2015, the hottest part of the Tokyo summer. Even at this hour the air was thick and warm, and the window stood open for any breeze that might come. In a few days Obon would begin. Obon is the time in August when, people believe, the dead come home. For three or four days families clean their graves, light small fires at the door to show the spirits the way, hang paper lanterns and leave food on the family altar. Then they send the dead back again. Many people were already leaving the city on crowded trains to visit their hometowns and family graves. The people who stayed were hanging lanterns in the shopping streets.
In most places Obon would only be a custom. In Japan in 2015 it was a little more than that. Everyone knew the veil was real, and everyone knew it grew thinner in this week.

The flat was in Kita, the north ward of Tokyo. Kita was not a famous part of the city. It was a place of narrow streets, old apartment blocks, small family shops and railway lines, with the wide Arakawa river along its northern edge. Most people who lived there had lived there a long time. Rei had lived there all his life, in this flat, on a hill above Ōji station, with his brother.

His brother was Uedera Gin. He was twenty-eight, nine years older than Rei, a tall man with long black hair that he wore loose past his jaw and never remembered to cut. Gin was a field officer for the Civil Veil Division.

Everyone in Japan knew what the Civil Veil Division was, the way they knew what the fire brigade was. Between the world of the living and the world of the dead there is a thin boundary, and people call it the veil. Usually it holds. Sometimes it grows thin, and things come through. Some of those things are only lost and sad. Some are dangerous. The Division was the government office that dealt with them. People called it the CVD. Its officers went into the houses and streets where the veil had gone wrong and put things right, or tried to.

So Gin kept strange hours. Everyone who knew him knew that. His work did not stop at five. But he called. He always called. Ten minutes late meant a message. An hour late meant a phone call and a voice saying, “Eat without me, I'm fine, go to bed.” In nineteen years he had never once let a night end without a word.

Rei checked his phone. No message. He checked it again, because lately he checked everything twice. The lock. The stove. The date. For a few weeks now the city had felt to him like a held breath, and he had told nobody, because there was nothing to tell. It was just a feeling. It was just a habit he did not like.

In the black glass of the window his own face looked back at him. Tired eyes. A jaw more like Gin's than his own. Rei, he thought, as if he needed the face in the glass to agree that this was his name. It agreed. He did not know why that felt like a relief.
He switched on the living-room lamp. He never did that at night. But lately the dark had started to feel as if it was paying attention, and he wanted it to stop.
Gin's door was shut. Rei knocked once, softly, feeling stupid, and opened it.

blocks.cap: Gin's room, the bed made and the desk lamp burning

blocks.p: The bed was made with square corners. The chair was pushed all the way under the desk. And the desk lamp was on. A small yellow circle of light lay on the bare wood, as if Gin had been working under it a minute ago and had stepped out to take a call. Nothing lay in the circle. No pen, no paper, no cup.

On the shelf above the desk stood the notebook Gin wrote in at night. He always closed it when Rei came near. Leaning against the base of the lamp was a photograph of the two of them years ago, squinting into the sun on some beach Rei could barely remember. Gin kept it where he could see it from the bed.

The room did not feel empty. It felt left behind. Rei could not tell if that was true, or if he was doing what Gin had always warned him about. Finding shapes in the quiet, because the quiet frightened him.
Back in the kitchen he filled the kettle and did not light the gas. Two cups sat upside down on the rack. Gin always set out two, though he was almost never home for the second.
Then Rei looked at the hook by the front door, and his stomach went cold.
Gin's keys were not on it.

The hook hung in the genkan. In a Japanese home the genkan is the small entrance just inside the front door, a step lower than the rest of the floor, where everyone takes off their shoes before stepping up into the house. Gin's keys had hung there every day since Rei was small enough to be lifted up to reach them. Gin put them on the hook first thing every morning, before coffee, before anything, the way some people touch a doorframe for luck. The brass hook was worn bright where his thumb went.
Rei had a private joke about it. Some mornings he slid the keys a few centimetres along the hook to see if Gin would notice. Gin never said a word. Rei had always taken that to mean he hadn't.
Now the hook was bare.
He crossed to the front door. It was not locked. It was not even shut. The latch rested against the frame without catching, and the door stood a finger's width open onto the night.
Rei had lived in this flat his whole life. He had never once known Gin to leave the door like that.

He pushed it open. Like most small apartment buildings in Tokyo, theirs had no inside hallway. Each front door opened onto a long concrete walkway along the outside of the building, with a railing on one side and the street below. The walkway was empty. The orange street lamp lit the railing, the bicycles parked below and the row of closed doors, exactly as it did every night. Two doors down, a neighbour's futon was still hung over the rail to air. Nothing moved. The city went on being large and ordinary and uninterested, and somehow that was worse than if something had moved.
Something glinted on the concrete just past the doorstep.

A key. A single brass door key on a plain ring, lying where a hand had dropped it or set it down. Rei crouched and picked it up. It was cold, properly cold, the cold of metal that has lain out all night. Beside it, crushed flat, lay the stub of a cigarette smoked exactly halfway.
It was Gin's brand. Gin smoked half a cigarette on the step every morning and then put it out, because Rei complained about the smell inside. He never smoked at night.

Rei looked left along the walkway, then right, then down to the street. Empty. Asleep. Perfect. There was nothing else at all, and that was the part that stayed with him afterward. How completely nothing else there was.
He went back inside and shut the door, and this time he heard the latch catch.
Only then did he see the book on the kitchen table. He must have walked past it twice.

It was Gin's archive. That was what Gin called it. It was a thick field book with soft corners, and Gin carried it everywhere, into places Rei was not allowed to know about and out again, year after year. Gin did not leave it on tables. He did not leave it anywhere. And yet here it lay, open, squared to the edge of the table, as if someone had wanted it found by the first person to sit down.
It was open at the first page. The handwriting was Gin's, small and exact, the print of a man who trusted ink more than memory. Rei read it standing up.

doc.title: Personal Archive. Opening Note
lines: If you found this: the keys were on the hook because I put them there. The lamp was on because I was working. The door was not quite closed because I heard something in the corridor and I looked up and then I kept writing and I forgot to go back and close it.

Whatever you are looking for... the world is in here. I documented everything I know. Six years of field work, case files, entity taxonomy, practitioner profiles, the political landscape of who controls what and why. The archive is complete. It functions without me.
Start at chapter one. Read in order the first time. The world builds on itself and some things will not make sense until other things do. The index is in the field kit, left pocket.
I was going to annotate the later sections more thoroughly. I ran out of time. The notes in the margins are the annotations. Read the margins.

blocks.p: Rei read it again. Then he looked up.
The lamp in Gin's room was burning. That part was true.
The front door had not been quite closed. That part was true.
The hook by the door was empty.

The note had been written for a night when Gin heard something outside, looked up, and went back to his writing. It had not been written for a night when he got up from the table and went out to see what it was.

Rei turned the page with a hand that was not quite steady. The next page was headed The World. It was dense, careful writing about openings and membranes, the kind of thing Gin said at dinner when he was tired and forgot who he was talking to. Halfway down, one sentence stopped Rei so hard that he put his palm flat on the table.

doc.title: Personal Archive. The World
lines: The archive you are reading is set in the Kita district of the city. A specific apartment. A desk lamp that was on because I was working. A field investigator's archive, open on the desk.
If you are reading this at 3:47 in the morning: that is approximately when Rei found it. That detail is in the archive for a reason. Keep reading.

blocks.p: He looked at the stove clock. It said 3:52.

He made himself think it through slowly. Either Gin had known, weeks or months ago, the exact hour of the exact night his brother would come to this table. Or somebody had written that line since. Rei did not know which was worse. He found he did not want to know yet.

He closed the book. He put it in his bag. He put the cold key in his pocket, where it stayed cold against his leg. Then he let himself think the sentence all the way to the end, the one he had been holding off since he saw the empty hook.
Something has happened to Gin.
There. It was in the room now. He could not put it back.

He could wait until morning. He could call the Division and let the proper people fail to find his brother. Nobody would blame him. Rei stood in the kitchen with the book heavy on his shoulder and knew he was not going to wait. He stepped down into the genkan and pushed his feet into his shoes without untying them, the way Gin always told him not to.
Itsuki answered his message before he reached the bottom of the stairs.

Kuroda Itsuki was awake. Itsuki was always awake at this hour, painting or writing code or both, and he had been Rei's best friend since they were twelve. Rei had typed four lines with his thumb while he locked the door. Gin didn't come home. Door was open. His key was on the walkway. I'm going down to Ōji.
I'm up, Itsuki wrote back. I was going to message you. He didn't answer me either, since Wednesday. Tell me what you need and I'll find it.

Rei did not need to say where he was going. They both knew Gin's way home. It ran down the long slope to the overpass at Ōji, and the overpass was the last place anyone could say for certain that Gin had been ordinary.

The street outside was warm and damp, like the inside of a mouth. Rei walked down the hill past houses with their shutters closed and their air conditioners dripping onto the pavement. Above the trees of Asukayama, the small park that rises on a hill beside Ōji station, the sky was still black. In the daytime Asukayama was full of children and old men playing shogi on benches. At this hour it was a dark shape with no sound in it at all. The cicadas had not started yet. In an hour they would be screaming in every tree.

blocks.cap: A konbini on a Kita corner before dawn

blocks.p: At the bottom of the slope a konbini glowed white on the corner. A konbini is a Japanese convenience store, small and bright and open all night, where people buy rice balls, coffee, stamps and phone credit at any hour. Through the glass Rei saw the young clerk asleep on his feet behind the counter, his head nodding. Someone had already taped a paper lantern by the door for Obon, white with blue writing. A newspaper delivery man went past on a small motorbike, the first of the morning, and did not look at Rei. Rei kept walking, and the light of the konbini fell away behind him.
Rei had crossed the Ōji overpass a thousand times without a thought. Tonight, halfway across, he walked into cold.

It was not a draught. It was a column of cold air that did not belong to August. It stood in the middle of the walkway like a person waiting for someone. The hair rose on his arms. Under the noise of the first delivery trucks he heard something very small. A sound like a child trying not to cough.
He stopped.

Something was caught there. He could not have said how he knew. It was the same way he knew when a room had just had an argument in it, or when a man on the train was about to cry. Gin called it noticing. Rei called it nothing at all, because it was just how his head worked.
The thing in the cold felt him notice it. It went very still, the way small animals go still when something large finally looks their way.
“It's all right,” Rei said under his breath, to nobody, to it. “I'm not going to do anything.”
He stood there with his hands in his pockets until the trucks had gone past. Slowly the cold grew thinner. Before it went, it let something go, the way a fist opens at the end.

It was not words. It was a picture, laid in his mind as clearly as a photograph. This bridge, at night. A man crossing it, walking north. The street lamp behind him. And his shadow falling the wrong way. A shadow should stretch away from the light. This one did not. It lay ahead of the man on the concrete, leading him, as if something walked half a second in front of the man it belonged to.
It was the night Gin stopped answering.
Then the cold was gone. The overpass was only an overpass, and Rei was standing in the middle of it with his heart beating hard.
He typed it into the notes on his phone before he could start doubting it. A man with the wrong shadow. Ōji overpass. The night Gin vanished.
Then he looked down.
The street lamp was behind him. His own shadow lay behind him too, long and thin, where a shadow belongs. He watched it for a long moment anyway, to be sure it stayed there.
His phone buzzed. It was Itsuki. Come to the studio. Don't walk back over the bridge.
A second message came a moment later. I think I've been painting it.
